metaDescription: Seven portable power stations under $1000 in the 1kWh class, compared by rated watts, surge, recharge speed, UPS switchover and battery cycle life.
expertTake: The EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic is the pick because it pairs 1800W of rated output with fast wall charging and a UPS-class switchover. The GRECELL 999Wh is the value pick when you only need small appliances and tools at a low price tier. Anyone planning to run a space heater, a full-size kettle on a long outage or a well pump should skip this class and look at a larger system.
introParagraphs: A power station is a battery, an inverter and a charger in one box, and the useful question is always the same: how many watts can it deliver at once, and how many hours can it keep delivering them. The battery sets the runtime and the inverter sets the ceiling.

This class sits in the middle of the market, large enough for a fridge and a router during an outage and small enough to carry to a campsite. Listing prices move, and the $1000 cap reflects prices when this guide was updated on 2026-11-07.

products.name: EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic 1024Wh, 1800W AC, UPS switchover
products.description:
The Delta 3 Classic pairs a 1024Wh battery with an 1800W inverter and a 3600W surge figure, which is the best balance of tank and pipe in this lineup. Its X-Stream wall charging takes it from empty to 80 percent in about 45 minutes, and a UPS switchover under 10 ms keeps a PC or router running when the grid drops. The 100W USB-C port can charge a laptop without the inverter.

Against the Bluetti Elite 100 V2 it matches the rating and charge time on paper, and against the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 it has 300W more continuous output. At 1800W it can run a kettle or a microwave for short bursts, but a 1024Wh tank empties in roughly half an hour at that load. For a fridge and a router it lasts many hours.

Ownership is mostly about storage and charging habits. Keep it at a partial charge when idle, switch the AC output off when unused so the inverter does not burn standby power, and match any solar panel to the input limits before you buy one.
products.bestFor: Home backup for a fridge and router plus short high-watt bursts.
pros: 1800W rated output with a 3600W surge figure
0 to 80 percent charge in about 45 minutes
UPS switchover under 10 ms protects PCs
100W USB-C charges laptops without the inverter
cons: 1024Wh tank empties fast at full 1800W load
Heavy for hand carrying over distance
Solar input limits need checking before panel purchase

products.name: Bluetti Elite 100 V2 1024Wh, 1800W AC, 10 ms UPS
products.description:
The Elite 100 V2 uses the same 1024Wh and 1800W pairing as the EcoFlow, with a 2700W Power Lifting mode that lets it run some heating loads at reduced output. The maker says it is 35 percent smaller than its earlier design, and a 1200W TurboBoost wall charge reaches 80 percent in roughly 45 minutes. A 10 ms UPS switchover keeps a router and PC alive through brief outages.

Against the EcoFlow it trades the 3600W surge figure for a 2700W lifting mode, which behaves differently, because lifting reduces output voltage or power to fit a heating load rather than delivering true surge. That is useful for a kettle but not for a motor start. It is the better fit if you care about footprint.

Ownership centers on the same lithium iron phosphate chemistry as the others. Expect a long cycle life, store it partly charged, and keep it out of hot cars and freezing garages.
products.bestFor: Home backup where a smaller body matters.
pros: 1800W rated with a 2700W Power Lifting mode
1200W TurboBoost wall charge to 80 percent in about 45 minutes
Built-in 10 ms UPS switchover for routers and PCs
Smaller body than the maker's earlier design
cons: Power Lifting is not true motor surge
Same 1024Wh tank empties fast at full load

products.name: DJI Power 1000 V2 1024Wh LFP, 37 minute charge to 80%
products.description:
The DJI Power 1000 V2 leads this lineup on recharge speed, reaching 80 percent in 37 minutes from the wall, with a 1024Wh LFP battery and a headline output of 2600W. It uses a smart battery management system and a sub-nano coating on the electronics for protection. The compact body is its other selling point.

The 2600W headline is the highest number in the guide, but read the listing for how it is delivered, because the EcoFlow and Bluetti state 1800W rated plus surge or lifting figures. Against both it recharges faster and is likely to be the better camp and van companion. For a router and fridge backup the EcoFlow also offers a stated UPS switchover.

Ownership is routine: partial charge storage, AC output off when idle, and care with solar input matching. Treat the 2600W as a ceiling for brief loads, not a constant rating.
products.bestFor: Camping and van use where recharge time matters.
pros: Highest headline output in the guide
cons: Headline output needs checking against rated output
No stated UPS switchover in the feature text
Short on documented port detail

products.name: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 1024Wh, 1500W, 3000W peak

specList.label: Ports
specList.value: 2 USB-C, 1 USB-A, 1 DC car, 2 pure sine AC

products.description:
The Explorer 1000 v2 offers 1500W with a 3000W peak, two pure sine AC outlets, two USB-C ports, one USB-A and a car port. It charges from 0 to 100 percent in 50 minutes, and a 10 ms UPS switchover covers short outages. The layout is straightforward and the pure sine output suits sensitive electronics.

Against the EcoFlow it gives up 300W of continuous output and 600W of surge, and against the DJI it recharges more slowly to 80 percent but promises a full charge in 50 minutes. It is the better pick for laptops, cameras and a router than for tools.

Ownership is simple with a mainstream brand and a familiar app. Keep the output off when idle and store it partly charged.

products.name: Jackery HomePower 1000 v2 1024Wh, 1500W, 10 ms UPS
products.description:
The HomePower 1000 v2 is a home-backup unit with a 10 ms UPS switchover, 3,000V surge resistance with a lightning shield, and a LiFePO4 battery rated for 6,000 plus cycles. The maker quotes a 16 year lifespan, which is a rated figure and not a promise. The target is a router, a modem and a PC that must stay up.

Against the Explorer 1000 v2 it is the home-oriented sibling with the surge shield and the cycle claim. Against the EcoFlow it gives up 300W of output but states a far longer cycle rating. It suits a desk or a closet more than a campsite.

Ownership favors it, since fewer cycles used means a longer life. Keep it plugged in as the maker describes, check the surge shield wiring and store it at partial charge if you unplug it for months.
products.bestFor: Whole-year home backup for networking gear and a PC.
pros: 10 ms UPS switchover for routers and PCs
cons: 1500W is below the 1800W units
Aimed at home use, less camp-friendly
Lifespan figures are rated, not guaranteed

products.name: Dabbsson 1000L 1008Wh semi-solid LiFePO4, 1200W AC
products.description:
The Dabbsson 1000L uses semi-solid LiFePO4 cells and says the chemistry gives 1.3 times the runtime of a standard pack. It delivers 1200W with a 1600W boost, a 100W USB-C port and a wall recharge to 80 percent in 50 minutes. It can take up to 600W of solar input.

Against the EcoFlow it has 600W less continuous output but accepts solar generously. The runtime claim is the maker's, and a larger pack still gives the same 1008Wh. Treat it as a mid-power camping and backup unit.

Ownership is similar to other LiFePO4 units, though semi-solid cells are newer and have less track record. Store it partly charged and keep it dry.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want generous solar input and moderate output.
cons: Semi-solid cells have a shorter track record
Runtime claim is the maker's own figure
600W less continuous output than the EcoFlow

products.name: GRECELL 999Wh power station, 1000W, 10 ports, 17 lb
products.description:
The GRECELL packs 999Wh into a 17 lb frame with 1000W continuous, a 2000W peak and ten ports including two AC outlets and a 60W USB-C. It uses an automotive-grade battery rated for 2000 plus cycles and a 10 year lifespan. The port count makes it a charging hub for a camp or a workshop.

Against the EcoFlow it has 800W less rated output and half the surge. Against the Dabbsson it has a similar tank but a lower boost. It is the value pick for phones, laptops, lights and small tools at a low price tier.

Ownership is basic: keep it partly charged in storage, run the inverter only when needed and do not push it near the 1000W limit for long. It lacks the stated UPS switchover of the premium units.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Rated continuous watts is the real limit, and surge only covers a brief startup. The EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic lists 1800W rated with 3600W surge, while the GRECELL lists 1000W with 2000W peak. Motor loads can need two to three times running watts at startup, so a fridge compressor fits a 1000W unit but a power tool may not.

Runtime is roughly capacity times 0.8 to 0.85 divided by load. A 1024Wh unit such as the DJI Power 1000 V2 delivers about 820 to 870Wh, so an 800W load lasts about an hour and a 100W load about eight. Buyers often pair a big inverter with a small tank and are surprised by the short run.

A UPS-class switchover keeps a PC or router running when the grid drops. The EcoFlow lists under 10 ms, the Bluetti lists 10 ms and both Jackery models list 10 ms, while the GRECELL and Dabbsson state none. If you want it for a desk, do not assume it exists.

Lithium iron phosphate cells give far more cycles than standard lithium-ion and tolerate heat better. The Jackery HomePower rates 6,000 plus cycles and the GRECELL 2000 plus. Ratings are the maker's figures, but a higher number tends to track a more conservative pack.

The DJI reaches 80 percent in 37 minutes and the EcoFlow and Bluetti in about 45, while the Jackery Explorer takes 50 minutes to full. Solar input varies, and the Dabbsson accepts 600W. Match panel voltage and connector to the input limits before buying panels.

An enabled AC inverter burns power with no load, so switch it off when unused. Store at roughly 40 to 60 percent charge and top up every few months. Do not charge below freezing or leave it in a hot car.

specDecoder.meaning: Watt-hours measure stored energy, the tank. Divide usable Wh by load watts for runtime.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Dabbsson lists 1008Wh and the GRECELL 999Wh, both about the same tank as the 1024Wh units.

specDecoder.meaning: Rated is what the inverter can deliver continuously. Surge covers a brief startup spike.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DJI lists a 2600W headline, so check how it is delivered against the EcoFlow 1800W.

specDecoder.meaning: The time the unit takes to switch to battery when grid power drops. Ten milliseconds or less keeps most PCs running.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EcoFlow and Bluetti list it, while the GRECELL does not.

specDecoder.meaning: A mode that runs heating loads at reduced output to fit the inverter. It is not true motor surge.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Bluetti lists 2700W lifting beside 1800W rated.

specDecoder.meaning: The number of full charge cycles before capacity drops to a stated level. LiFePO4 gives thousands.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Jackery HomePower lists 6,000 plus and the GRECELL lists 2000 plus.

howWeEvaluated.title: Rated output
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated each listing for rated continuous watts before surge. The EcoFlow and Bluetti at 1800W led, followed by the Jackery pair at 1500W. Units with only headline numbers, like the DJI at 2600W, were scored with a note.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tank and runtime
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared watt-hours and worked out realistic runtime at common loads. Every unit here sits near 1000Wh, so the difference is the inverter. The Dabbsson at 1008Wh and GRECELL at 999Wh match the others.

howWeEvaluated.title: Backup behavior
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked for stated UPS switchover and surge protection. The EcoFlow, Bluetti and both Jackery units list it, and the HomePower adds a 3kV shield. We treated missing claims as not present.

howWeEvaluated.title: Recharge and solar
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at wall recharge time and solar input from the spec sheet. The DJI at 37 minutes led on speed, and the Dabbsson at 600W led on solar intake.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cycle life and upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We read cycle ratings and storage guidance from owner feedback patterns and the spec sheet. LiFePO4 units were credited, with the Jackery HomePower at 6,000 plus on top.

howToChoose.intro: Tiers are relative within the cap.

cards.label: Camp and van
cards.text: The DJI Power 1000 V2, GRECELL and Dabbsson suit portable use with fast recharge, many ports and solar input. They matter when you recharge from panels or a car.

cards.label: Home backup
cards.text: The EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic, Bluetti Elite 100 V2 and Jackery HomePower list UPS switchover. They keep a router and PC alive through an outage.

howToChoose.note: Camp buyers pick DJI or GRECELL. Home buyers pick the EcoFlow or the Jackery HomePower.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a stated UPS switchover, enough rated watts for a fridge, and a battery that tolerates a partial charge in storage. Heating loads exceed this class.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic is the best fit, with 1800W and under 10 ms switchover. The Jackery HomePower adds a surge shield for networking gear.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you need to run a space heater, a well pump or a fridge through a multi-day outage. This class tops out near 1800W and 1024Wh, so larger systems are the next step.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you mostly charge phones and laptops. The GRECELL covers them with ten ports at the lowest tier in the lineup.

maintenance.why: A pack held full or empty ages faster. Aim for 40 to 60 percent.
An enabled inverter burns standby power. Turn it off to keep the charge.
Loose ports and frayed cords cause heat. Inspect before long loads.
Voltage and connector mismatches cause no charge. Check the input limits.

maintenance.task: Keep out of heat and frost
maintenance.why: Do not charge below freezing or leave it in a hot car.

faq.q: EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic or Bluetti Elite 100 V2?
faq.a: Both pair 1024Wh with 1800W and a UPS switchover. The EcoFlow lists a 3600W surge and the Bluetti a smaller body with 2700W Power Lifting. Pick on size and surge needs.

faq.q: Is under $1000 enough for a good power station?
faq.a: Yes for a fridge, router and small appliances. This class holds about 1000Wh, which is hours for light loads and under an hour for heating loads.

faq.q: How long will a 1024Wh unit run my fridge?
faq.a: A fridge averages far below its compressor rating, so several hours to about a day is typical. Measure the real draw with a plug-in watt meter.
Prefer it. LiFePO4 gives thousands of cycles and tolerates heat better than standard lithium-ion, though it is heavier.

faq.q: Can I run a space heater on this class?
faq.a: Not for long. Heaters draw 1500W and drain a 1024Wh tank in under an hour, and some exceed the rated output.

faq.q: Does a 2600W headline mean it runs 2600W?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Check whether it is rated continuous or a boost figure, and size loads to the continuous number.
